questions.q: The probability of an impossible event is:
questions.solution:
$P = \mathbf{0}$ for something that cannot happen, and $1$ for something certain.

Every probability lies between the two: $0 \le P \le 1$. An answer outside that range is always an error.

$P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A) = \mathbf{0.7}$.

Either it happens or it does not, so the two probabilities must add to 1. This is often the quickest route to an answer — especially for 'at least one'.

questions.q: Two fair coins are tossed. The probability of two heads is:
questions.solution:
The tosses are independent, so multiply: $\dfrac12 \times \dfrac12 = \mathbf{\dfrac14}$.

The four equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT, and only one of them is two heads.

questions.q: For mutually exclusive events $A$ and $B$, $P(A \text{ or } B)$ equals:
questions.solution:
Mutually exclusive means they cannot both happen, so there is no overlap to subtract:

$P(A \text{ or } B) = \mathbf{P(A) + P(B)}$.

**Remember: 'or' adds, 'and' multiplies** — provided the events are exclusive for the first and independent for the second.

questions.q: A drawing pin is dropped $200$ times and lands point up $130$ times. The relative frequency of landing point up is:
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{130}{200} = \mathbf{0.65}$.

Relative frequency is an **estimate** of probability from experiment, used when outcomes are not equally likely — and a drawing pin is exactly such a case. The more trials, the better the estimate.

questions.q: A bag holds $5$ red and $3$ blue balls. Find the probability of drawing a red ball, correct to three decimal places.
Two fair dice are thrown. Find the probability that both show a six, correct to four decimal places.
The probability that a seed germinates is $0.8$. Two seeds are sown. Find the probability that at least one germinates.
questions.solution:
Work through the complement:

$P(\text{neither}) = 0.2 \times 0.2 = 0.04$

$P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - 0.04 = \mathbf{0.96}$.

Counting the one way it fails is always easier than counting the several ways it succeeds.

questions.q: A bag holds $4$ red and $6$ blue balls. Two are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that both are red, correct to four decimal places.
questions.solution:
$\dfrac{4}{10} \times \dfrac{3}{9} = \dfrac{12}{90} = \dfrac{2}{15} \approx \mathbf{0.1333}$.

**Both** numbers change on the second draw: one fewer red, and one fewer ball altogether. That is the whole difference between with and without replacement.

questions.q: A fair die is thrown $180$ times. Find the expected number of fours.
questions.solution:
$180 \times \dfrac16 = \mathbf{30}$.

'Expected' does not mean it will happen — it is the long-run average. An actual run of 180 throws might give 26 or 34 and be entirely unremarkable.

questions.q: A bag holds $3$ red and $5$ green sweets. Two are taken without replacement. Draw the tree diagram in words and find the probability that the two sweets are of different colours.
questions.solution:
**First draw:** $P(R) = \tfrac38$, $P(G) = \tfrac58$.

**Second draw**, with 7 sweets left:

• After red: $P(R) = \tfrac27$, $P(G) = \tfrac57$

• After green: $P(R) = \tfrac37$, $P(G) = \tfrac47$

**The four branches** (multiply along each):

$P(RR) = \tfrac38 \times \tfrac27 = \tfrac{6}{56}$

$P(RG) = \tfrac38 \times \tfrac57 = \tfrac{15}{56}$

$P(GR) = \tfrac58 \times \tfrac37 = \tfrac{15}{56}$

$P(GG) = \tfrac58 \times \tfrac47 = \tfrac{20}{56}$

**Check:** the four add to $\tfrac{56}{56} = 1$ ✓

**Different colours** means $RG$ **or** $GR$, so add those two:

$\tfrac{15}{56} + \tfrac{15}{56} = \mathbf{\dfrac{30}{56} = \dfrac{15}{28}} \approx 0.536$.

**Multiply along the branches, add between them** — that single sentence is the whole method.

questions.q: In a class of 30 students, 18 study French, 15 study Spanish and 7 study both. Find the probability that a student chosen at random studies neither language.
questions.solution:
**Use the addition rule**, subtracting the overlap so it is not counted twice:

$n(F \text{ or } S) = 18 + 15 - 7 = 26$.

**Neither:** $30 - 26 = 4$ students.

$P(\text{neither}) = \dfrac{4}{30} = \mathbf{\dfrac{2}{15}} \approx 0.133$.

**Checking with a Venn diagram:**

• French only: $18 - 7 = 11$

• Both: $7$

• Spanish only: $15 - 7 = 8$

• Neither: $4$

$11 + 7 + 8 + 4 = 30$ ✓

Filling in the **overlap first** and working outwards makes every Venn question straightforward — the trouble always comes from counting the middle twice.

questions.q: A box holds $7$ white and $3$ black counters. Three counters are drawn without replacement. Find the probability that all three are white, and the probability that exactly one is black.
questions.solution:
**All three white:**

$\dfrac{7}{10} \times \dfrac{6}{9} \times \dfrac{5}{8} = \dfrac{210}{720} = \mathbf{\dfrac{7}{24}} \approx 0.292$.

**Exactly one black.** The black counter could be the first, second or third draw.

Each order has the same probability — the numerators are the same three numbers in a different sequence, and the denominators are always $10 \times 9 \times 8$:

$P(BWW) = \dfrac{3}{10} \times \dfrac{7}{9} \times \dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{126}{720}$

$P(WBW) = \dfrac{7}{10} \times \dfrac{3}{9} \times \dfrac{6}{8} = \dfrac{126}{720}$

$P(WWB) = \dfrac{7}{10} \times \dfrac{6}{9} \times \dfrac{3}{8} = \dfrac{126}{720}$

**Total:**

$3 \times \dfrac{126}{720} = \dfrac{378}{720} = \mathbf{\dfrac{21}{40}} = 0.525$.

**The insight worth keeping:** order does not change the probability, only the arrangement — so work out **one** order and multiply by the number of arrangements.

questions.q: Explain the difference between theoretical probability and relative frequency, and say when each is used.
questions.solution:
**Theoretical probability** is worked out by reasoning about equally likely outcomes:

$P(\text{event}) = \dfrac{\text{favourable outcomes}}{\text{total outcomes}}$

It needs no experiment — a fair die gives $P(6) = \tfrac16$ before it is ever thrown.

**Relative frequency** is found from experiment:

$\dfrac{\text{number of times it happened}}{\text{number of trials}}$

**When each is used.**

• Theoretical probability works only when the outcomes are **equally likely** — coins, fair dice, cards, balls in a bag.

• Relative frequency is needed when they are **not**, or when the situation cannot be analysed: a drawing pin landing point up, a biased die, the chance of rain, the failure rate of a machine.

**The connection.** As the number of trials grows, the relative frequency settles down towards the true probability — the **law of large numbers**.

Ten throws of a fair die might give three sixes; ten thousand will give very close to a sixth. This is also how bias is detected: a die whose relative frequency stays far from $\tfrac16$ over many throws is not fair.

questions.q: A game costs $\$2$ to play. A player throws a fair die and wins $\$9$ for a six and nothing otherwise. Determine whether the game is fair.
questions.solution:
**Expected winnings per game:**

$P(\text{six}) = \tfrac16$, winning $\$9$; $P(\text{not six}) = \tfrac56$, winning $\$0$.

Expected win $= \tfrac16 \times 9 + \tfrac56 \times 0 = \dfrac{9}{6} = \$1.50$.

**Cost to play:** $\$2$.

**Expected profit per game:** $1.50 - 2 = \mathbf{-\$0.50}$.

The game is **not fair** — the player loses $50$ cents per game on average, so over 100 games the organiser expects to take about $\$50$.

**To make it fair**, the prize would have to be $\$12$: $\tfrac16 \times 12 = \$2$, exactly the stake.

'Fair' in probability has a precise meaning — an expected profit of **zero** — and no commercial game is ever fair in that sense, because the organiser's margin is the difference.
